rv.q: The angry confrontation that ensues between Nelson and Nick has a bruising, brutal power.

The cultural specificity in Leguizamo’s work is airtight, and in his first effort at writing for a full cast, he clears two important hurdles: a good ear for dialogue and an understanding that everyone needs strong intentions.
The play itself, however, is a mess.
What Leguizamo achieves, fortunately, is far greater: a true American tragedy.
The production now at The Public Theater is a vigorous evening in the theater which should provoke talk and discussion.
With The Other Americans, he digs deep into the traumas and expectations driving American men to both success and ruin...
If the script aspires to more than it ultimately achieves, the production is solid and satisfying even before any of the seven cast members step out on stage...
To borrow a metaphor from the playwright’s beloved New York Mets, The Other Americans is a big swing.
While best known as an actor, Mr. Leguizamo, who first gained attention as a standup comedian, has crafted acclaimed solo shows, among them “Freak” and “Latin History for Morons.”
Still, this is a case of a great unruly artist, whose best work has the untamed energy of slam poetry, dedicating himself a little too much to coloring inside the lines.
In the end, for all its ethnic flavor and emotional sound and fury, The Other Americans proves to be a surprisingly familiar domestic drama.
The story ambles, rather than surprises.
Though Leguizamo is admirable on stage, The Other Americans too often feels more like a thought experiment than a fully distinct riff on "the lie of the American dream" play.
Sadly, “The Other Americans” makes a less convincing case for this claim that Leguizamo’s previous solo works.
The characters may be Latino, but the story itself would seem to owe much of its inspiration to the likes of Arthur Miller's Death of a Salesman or Eugene O'Neill's Long Day's Journey Into Night .

It is curious that The Public Theater and Arena Stage agreed to co-produce his unwieldy drama, but likely they are supporting Leguizamo’s continued development as an artist, which is the right thing to do although it proves to be not so rewarding an experience for viewers.

Lequizamo has written a new classic, bringing the common man archetype into the Hispanic community, revealing both its uniqueness and its universality, because of course Nelson is an uncommon common man, fighting his way to obscurity.
The positives far outweigh the negatives here though, and with Nelson Castro, Leguizamo aspires to create a tragic patriarch on a level with Willy Loman, Troy Maxson and James Tyrone.
Ruben Santiago-Hudson’s neat and compact direction keeps the action moving, never letting the audience miss a beat.
Leguizamo’s The Other Americans at the Public Theater NYC has all the makings of a resonant family tragedy, and when it locks into the volatile father–son dynamic, the play brushes against greatness.
Structurally, the ending felt very abrupt, and it was performed at a different pace than the rest of the show.
The elements of a great American drama are here, but they are assembled in a scattershot way that doesn’t quite cohere.
As an actor, Leguizamo harnesses his signature charm and social commentary, but as a playwright, The Other Americans drowns in its own exposition.
Yet the play is unsatisfying and much of the story is predictable.
Mr. Leguizamo provides a superficial and predictable script, that provides absolutely no character development.
The show eventually gets bogged down by genre clichés and clearly targeted plot twists, and it takes 135 minutes (including intermission) instead of a half hour (including commercials).

cn.t: Leguizamo's ambitious departure from solo comedy into Arthur Miller-style family tragedy earns mixed reviews. Critics praise his performance and emotional depth, but many find the traditional drama over-ambitious and underpowered.

vr.q: It's hard to make a fresh and original drama, but it's also hard to fault solid writing, acting, and direction. And ultimately, that's what won me over.
Overall, The Other Americans is a worthwhile evening of theater.
